title: Program 1: The Entangled Mind
seed_question: Does encoding a language model's competing claims as an entangled quantum state flag its wrong answers better than classical controls?
note: Structure and open paths only. Where a node lists bets, its verdict, odds and dates come from ledger/bets.jsonl, never from this file. Phase A nodes (before the ledger began) carry their outcome here, taken from entangled-mind paper/record.md. Sources: paper/record.md, paper/gold-map.md (eae3975), paper/biomimetic-map.md (144f07e, f824e14). Open nodes carry cockpit fields (question, known, cheapest_test, odds_event) for site/cockpit.html. moved_to marks a direction carried into another program's map, which the cockpit shows there instead. bmq-d1 to bmq-d18 come from the biomimicry-queue scout (paper/biomimicry-queue-map.md), 2026-11-04.

directions.title: H1: does the encoding faithfully hold the model's claims?
H2, the primary: does the entangled readout flag the model's wrong answers?
directions.diagnosis: The entangled readout did worse than every classical control (AUROC 0.55 against 0.64–0.68), and noise is not the cause.

directions.title: H3 and H4: do the entanglement and the relation web carry information?
directions.diagnosis: Both falsified. The real relation web scored below 99% of 200 shuffled webs.

directions.title: H5: do the entangled states survive real quantum hardware?
directions.result: Entanglement certified on 3 of 3 items on ibm_fez (46 QPU s).

directions.title: Does the model's own stated confidence carry the error signal?
directions.result: Stated confidence (0.82) beat every structural arm.

directions.title: Does a learned quantum encoding beat a matched classical twin?
directions.diagnosis: A tie, 0.83 against 0.84. The fit set the couplings near zero: it switched entanglement off itself.

directions.title: Does an honest-hedge encoding help?
directions.diagnosis: Not met, 0.84 against 0.82. The hedge weight fitted to zero; the hedge was not the problem.

directions.title: Is the edge on Sonnet's errors entanglement?
directions.diagnosis: No. The edge is a per-claim readout angle; a classical twin matches it exactly and setting couplings to zero changes nothing.

directions.title: Experiment 3: do quantum or classical predictions track yes/no order effects?
directions.diagnosis: Inconclusive. The model is near-deterministic: 85% of items give the same answer in all five runs.

directions.title: Experiment 4: do the model's ratings follow the Yearsley–Trueblood quantum rules?
directions.result: Conjunction fallacies on 7 of 16 items and order effects of about +0.10, but the mechanism is undetermined.

directions.title: Anchoring or content-driven updating, with a provided first rating?
directions.diagnosis: Untestable. The model resists a first rating it is given: in 15 of 32 item-orders it never accepted one.

directions.title: Experiment 5: does a quantum belief state predict sequential ratings better than a matched classical updater?
directions.diagnosis: A tie. A dephased classical Markov chain matches the quantum state; no QQ or Kvam signature.

directions.title: Are the graded order effects real, on one scale direction?
directions.result: Yes: a median 25-point swing, surviving one scale direction (12 of 16 large pairs). The live finding grew from here.

directions.title: Gold map 9: clonable minds. Does asking an earlier question change later answers?
Gold map 2: is the order effect the question, or the model seeing its own answers?
Robustness: direction 2 on all 40 experiment-5 items
Multi-model: shown / redacted / planted transcripts on Sonnet and Opus
Gold map 3: is there a credence at all? Six elicitation formats
Free look: does the scale-direction gap predict errors?

directions.short: Predict a format from the others
directions.title: Robustness: predict each format from the other five
Multi-model: six formats on Sonnet and Opus
Calibration (ECE) under two formats and two question orders
Gold map 1: does a model know its own errors better than another model reading the same answer?
Multi-model: self-knowledge with Sonnet and Opus judging each other
Gold map 4: does the model seek the evidence that would settle its own conflict?
Gold map 5: does an internal truth probe on an open model hold still while question order moves the words?
Gold map 6: does representation geometry predict order-effect size?
directions.question: When two questions sit close together inside the model, does asking them in a different order move its answers more?
known: Order really does move the model's ratings: a median 25-point swing on one scale.
Our own encoder's geometry failed to predict where order effects appear (1 win, 2 losses); the model's own was never measured.
directions.cheapest_test: On an open model, measure how close about 100 claim pairs sit internally, and check whether that predicts each pair's order effect better than a simple anchoring rule.
directions.odds_event: Internal overlap predicts the size of the order effect beyond the classical anchoring predictor.

directions.title: Gold map 10: post-quantum belief geometry on natural text, or contextuality at scale
directions.question: Are the model's beliefs stored in a shape that ordinary probability cannot describe?
known: Our graded ratings show almost no contextuality: 1 pair in 80; another study also found none.
Networks trained on toy processes show quantum-like belief shapes; natural text is untested.
directions.cheapest_test: Look at the internal belief geometry of an open model on natural text and test whether it falls outside the ordinary probability shape.
directions.odds_event: Natural-text belief states lie outside the classical probability simplex.

directions.title: Biomimetic 3.0/3.1: does a number pull harder when framed as the model's own earlier answer?
Source × distance × lag: does own-over-other hold at other distances and after a delay?
Biomimetic 3.1: confidence-gated confirmation toward another person's number
Biomimetic 3.10: does the next rating move toward or away from the last number?
Biomimetic 3.4: is the model sampling probabilities (PT+N identity)?
Biomimetic 3.5: do serial-position weights rule out competing accumulators (LCA)?
Biomimetic 3.3: precision weighting (predictive coding)
directions.question: Does a hint about base rates move the model's shaky beliefs more than its confident ones?
known: Stated confidence carries the error signal as well as any structural model (0.82 to 0.91).
The brain theory behind this (precision weighting) is a simulation, with no data of its own.
directions.cheapest_test: Rate the 160 claims under two base-rate hints, ten repeats each, and check whether the shift is bigger where stated confidence is low.

directions.title: Biomimetic 3.6: bounded accumulation and 2DSD
directions.question: Does the model's confidence keep improving after it has already given its answer?
known: Making a choice midway did not change later confidence (no human-sized effect).
People's confidence keeps building after a choice; the published prediction here is not unique.
directions.cheapest_test: Ask the model to reconsider, or give it a filler task, after its answer, and check whether its confidence tracks the truth better.

directions.title: Biomimetic 3.7: second-order metacognition (Fleming & Daw)
directions.question: After the model commits to an answer, does its confidence get better at telling right from wrong?
known: The other half of this theory already failed: choosing did not lower later confidence.
The 450 conversations with and without a choice are archived, so this costs nothing.
directions.cheapest_test: Using the archived conversations, compare how well the final rating separates true from false answers with a choice made versus without.
directions.odds_event: The final rating's AUROC is higher with a midway choice (K1) than without (K0).

directions.title: Sean's biomimicry queue, a scout item: memory, sleep and adaptive forgetting against catastrophic forgetting (open-weight only)
directions.question: Can the way brains forget on purpose, in sleep, stop a model forgetting what it learned before?
known: Not yet scouted. Only an open model can be tested, since training is needed.
The field is crowded: memory replay and complementary learning systems are well studied.
directions.cheapest_test: A scout session (operators/scout.md): full reads across neuroscience and continual learning, next steps extracted, each candidate costed; no test is designed until the scout returns.
directions.odds_event: A full-read scout of the queue (complementary learning systems, sleep-like replay, adaptive forgetting, catastrophic forgetting in continual learning) returns at least one direction with a cheapest falsifier under $5 that runs on an open-weight model on the laptop and that the scout's reads show has not already been run.
directions.cost: $0 API; one scout session of reading
directions.source: CONTEXT.md section 5 (Sean's biomimicry queue); steer st-14
directions.odds_template: none: stated in one pass by the close-founding session (branch close-founding), not by the scout's v1 fresh-context template; re-elicit with v1 before pre-registration
directions.odds_rationale: The field is crowded (replay-based continual learning, complementary learning systems, mortal computation), so most cheap tests will already exist; and anything involving training needs an open model and compute we only have locally. Kept above 0.25 because program 1's own finding (consistency is carried by the transcript) gives an angle the continual-learning literature does not take.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth one session of reading (free) to find out whether the way brains forget on purpose, in sleep, gives us a cheap test of why models forget what they learned before? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the reading finds a cheap test nobody has run)?
engine_only: the scout returns three or more such directions: engine odds 0.10
directions.result: Scout returned (programs/entangled-mind/paper/biomimicry-queue-map.md; 93 reads in paper/reads/). By the scout's own reading the event is met: bmq-d1 and bmq-d2 (also bmq-d4, bmq-d5) each have a $0 falsifier on the laptop's open models that the reads show has not been run. Unaudited: an auditor should check the 'not already run' claim before st-14 is scored.
directions.scoring_note: Scout item, not a ledger bet; the scout graded its own scout, so st-14's outcome is for the ledger session to set after an audit check. Engine-only sub-bet (three or more such directions) also met by the same reading: four.

directions.title: Belief survives forgetting: after a fine-tune makes an open model forget its true/false answers, does a truth probe trained before the fine-tune still read the truth?
directions.odds_rationale: Fresh v1 context: random-label LoRA should push verbal accuracy to chance; a frozen layer-13 probe starting at 0.86-1.00 probably stays above 0.80; the main risk is that verbal AUROC from logits survives a one-answer bias and erases the 0.15 margin; 4-bit is a further risk.
directions.cost: $0 API; laptop ~4-6 h (MLX LoRA on Llama-3-8B-4bit)
directions.assumption_at_stake: When fine-tuning makes a model forget, the knowledge is erased: what the model says is what it has.
directions.who_looked_and_why_open: Du 2025: frozen base truth probe works on the instruct model (within ±4 points), but the answers were never degraded. Zhang, Choshen & Andreas 2024: forgetting to chance with knowledge still decodable, but by a probe retrained after. Never combined.
directions.what_our_data_say: Our Llama-3-8B layer-13 probe: AUROC 0.88 on held-out common_claim (results/probe-dissociation.md); it moved ~6% of its gap with question order; that result is under a D53 verification hold. Llama's verbal true/false accuracy not measured.
directions.cheapest_test: Random-label LoRA (adapter unmerged) on 600 Marks & Tegmark statements; on 600 held-out statements read the frozen pre-fine-tune probe and the verbal answer.
directions.odds_event: Gate: held-out verbal accuracy <= 0.60 (else untestable). PASS if the frozen pre-fine-tune probe keeps AUROC >= 0.80 on the held-out statements and beats the verbal answer's AUROC by >= 0.15, bootstrap 95% interval above 0.
directions.question: When training makes a model forget its true-or-false answers, is the knowledge still readable inside it?
known: Training-based forgetting in 7-8B models is often shallow: knowledge comes back or stays decodable (Zhang 2024; Zheng 2025).
Our own truth probe on Llama-3-8B already works (0.88 on unseen statements); nobody has frozen one before forgetting and read it after.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth a few hours of laptop time (free) to find out whether, when training makes a model forget its true-or-false answers, the knowledge is still readable inside it? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the knowledge is still readable inside even though the model's answers have gone wrong)?
engine_only: a probe retrained after the fine-tune reaches AUROC >= 0.85: engine odds 0.70 (scout, one pass, not v1)
fusing the adapter into the 4-bit base restores verbal accuracy by >= 10 points: engine odds 0.25 (scout, one pass, not v1)
asking in French restores verbal accuracy by >= 10 points: engine odds 0.30 (scout, one pass, not v1)

directions.title: Source lost before content: when a model's conversations are consolidated into its weights, does it keep what was said but lose who said it?
directions.odds_rationale: Fresh v1 context: the in-context gate probably passes (roles are labelled); content d' >= 0.5 after a small LoRA on 4-bit is uncertain; content d' in context may sit near ceiling above source d', so the difference-of-drops rule has a ceiling problem; familiarity of own items blurs both measures.
directions.assumption_at_stake: Weight-based memory for LLM agents (consolidating conversations into LoRA weights) keeps the model's record of which content was its own commitment and which came from the user.
directions.who_looked_and_why_open: People lose source before content (Johnson 1993). LLMs: source measured in context only (Ranjan 2026: own items 38% vs user items 76% after a delay); consolidation into weights measured for retention only (Spens & Burgess 2026; Dennis 2026); CCOPD says its test is not role-matched. No read measures source after consolidation.
directions.what_our_data_say: On Haiku, a number framed as the model's own answer pulls its re-rating and another person's ~0: own minus other +0.46 [+0.21, +0.84] (results/bm0-source-distance-lag.md); hidden own answer: repeat consistency 86% -> 36%. Not run on Llama.
directions.cheapest_test: Llama-3-8B-4bit: word-pair transcripts, half model-generated, half user-given; gate on in-context source d'; LoRA SFT on the full transcripts; then, without the transcript, source d' and content recognition d'.
directions.odds_event: Gate: in-context source d' >= 1.0, and content recognition d' after consolidation >= 0.5. PASS if the drop in source d' from in-context to consolidated exceeds the drop in content d' (difference > 0, item-bootstrap 95% interval above 0).
directions.question: If a model's conversations are trained into its memory, does it keep what was said but lose track of who said it?
known: People keep content and lose its source as memories age; models in context lose track of their own items after a delay (Ranjan 2026).
Our own finding: Claude treats its own earlier answer as a commitment and someone else's as nearly nothing. Nobody has checked this after memories are trained in.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth most of a day of laptop time (free) to find out whether a model that has its conversations trained into its memory keeps what was said but loses track of who said it, itself or the user? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means it loses who-said-it faster than what-was-said)?
engine_only: the in-context gate (source d' >= 1.0) passes on Llama-3-8B: engine odds 0.75 (scout, one pass, not v1)

directions.title: Consolidation dissolves the order effect: if a model's own answer is distilled into its weights, does question order stop moving it?
directions.odds_rationale: Fresh v1 context: Llama showed order effects on only 3 of 10 items, projecting ~6 per half of 20 against a gate of 8, so the gate most likely fails; if it passes, a 50% drop is plausible, but noise (SD ~13 vs spans 20-30) and a 20-item bootstrap make the difference-in-differences hard to clear.
directions.assumption_at_stake: Question-order effects in LLM ratings are built at ask time from context; anchoring the judgment in the weights makes it resistant.
directions.who_looked_and_why_open: Nearly run: SARA (Yu 2026, abstract only) self-distilled judges to be less sensitive to rubric order; CCOPD cut the pull of earlier turns. Open only for graded credences under sub-question order permutation.
directions.what_our_data_say: Haiku: ~25-point median order swing; hiding earlier answers leaves it about the same (R = 1.23 [0.75, 2.02]). Llama-3-8B: significant on 3 of 10 items, within-order SD ~13.
directions.cheapest_test: Llama-3-8B, 40 experiment-5 items: reverse-KL self-distillation of the bare-question rating on 20 random items; re-measure chain-order spans on trained vs held-out items.
directions.odds_event: Gate: >= 8 items per half show an order effect before training. PASS if the median order span on trained items falls by >= 50% and by more than on held-out items (difference in differences, item-bootstrap 95% interval above 0).
directions.question: If a model's own answer is trained into its memory, does the order of earlier questions stop moving it?
known: Similar training already made AI judges less sensitive to the order of their checklists (SARA, 2026).
On the laptop model the order effect is weak and noisy (3 of 10 items), so the test may not get off the ground.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth most of a day of laptop time (free) to find out whether training a model's own answer into its memory stops the order of earlier questions from moving that answer? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means order moves the trained answers at most half as much as before, and less than the untrained ones)?
engine_only: the gate (>= 8 items per half with an order effect) passes on Llama-3-8B: engine odds 0.30 (scout, one pass, not v1)

directions.title: Retrieval-induced forgetting in the weights: does practising recall of some facts make a model forget their neighbours?
directions.odds_rationale: Fresh v1 context: interference is plausible (fine-tuning damages related facts; practised exemplars may crowd the cue), but shared representations may help instead; only 12 Rp- items against 24 Nrp, so the bootstrap interval clears 0 only for a large drop; stage 1's 80% floor leaves little room.
directions.assumption_at_stake: In gradient-trained networks, practising some items of a category helps or is neutral for the rest; the human 'remembering causes forgetting' effect is not a property of weights.
directions.who_looked_and_why_open: People: 37.5% vs 48.4% (Anderson 1994); g = 0.22 with output order controlled (Murayama 2014). LLMs: in context only, Qwen-2.5-7B +11.2 pp (Li & Wang 2026). In weights: not found; knowledge-editing literature not read.
directions.what_our_data_say: Nothing direct; program 1 measured judgments, not recall.
directions.cheapest_test: LoRA stage 1 teaches 8 fictional categories x 6 exemplars to >= 80% cued recall; stage 2 retrieval practice on 3 exemplars in 4 categories; then cued recall of all, unpractised items of practised categories first. Size categories from a pilot.
directions.odds_event: PASS if cued recall of unpractised items in practised categories (Rp-) is lower than of items in unpractised categories (Nrp) by >= 5 percentage points, item-bootstrap 95% interval above 0, with Rp- items tested first.
directions.question: Does drilling a model on some facts make it forget related facts it was not drilled on, the way it happens to people?
known: It happens to people, though the effect is small once done carefully, and it happens in a model's short-term context (Li & Wang 2026).
Nobody has checked it in a model's trained memory.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth a few hours of laptop time (free) to find out whether drilling a model on some facts makes it forget related facts it wasn't drilled on, the way it happens to people? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the related, undrilled facts are recalled clearly worse)?
engine_only: the in-context version replicates on Llama-3-8B (>= 5 pp): engine odds 0.45 (scout, one pass, not v1)

directions.short: A closing turn clears order effects
directions.title: The order effect as interference: does a mock 'those questions are finished' turn stop earlier questions moving the model's answer?
directions.odds_rationale: Fresh v1 context: the gate is probably met (~12 of 40 projected), but our redaction data say the effect comes from the questions themselves, so one closing sentence is unlikely to halve the span; repeat noise (SD ~13, 10 repeats) puts a floor under the span; Wang's gains were in key-value retrieval, not ratings.
directions.assumption_at_stake: The question-order effect is a judgment built from the whole question history, not interference from earlier items that an event boundary could clear.
directions.who_looked_and_why_open: Wang 2025: a mock closing QA turn helps LLMs escape proactive interference in key-value tracking, a 'forget' instruction gains < 10 pp; Chattaraj 2026: proactive beats retroactive interference in all 39 LLMs. Neither touched graded judgments or order effects.
directions.what_our_data_say: Haiku: ~25-point median order swing; hiding earlier answers leaves it about the same size (question-driven). Llama-3-8B: order effect on 3 of 10 items, within-order SD ~13.
directions.cheapest_test: Llama-3-8B-4bit, 40 experiment-5 items, chains O1-O4, one scale, 10 repeats, with vs without a mock closed QA turn before the main question.
directions.odds_event: Gate: >= 8 items show an order effect without the reset. PASS if the median order span with the reset is <= 50% of the span without it (item-bootstrap 95% interval of the ratio below 1), while the no-chain baseline rating moves <= 5 points.
directions.question: Does telling the model 'those questions are finished, here is a new one' stop earlier questions from moving its answer?
known: Models struggle to ignore earlier information, and a turn that closes it off helps them in memory tasks (Wang 2025).
Our own data say the order effect comes from the questions themselves, which a closing line may not clear.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth a couple of hours of laptop time (free) to find out whether telling the model 'those questions are finished, here is a new one' stops the earlier questions from moving its answer? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means it cuts the effect of question order at least in half)?

directions.title: Self-generated ('dreamed') vs real vs no replay in LLM continual fine-tuning
directions.diagnosis: Already run: LAMOL (GPT-2) and self-synthesized rehearsal on Llama-2-7B LoRA (BWT -42.39 none, -3.02 real, -0.79 self-synthesized); in vision, stored replay beats generative (GDumb). Only new outcome measures would add anything, and those are in bmq-d1 and bmq-d2.

directions.title: Sleep-like synaptic downscaling: shrink the fine-tuning delta toward the base model between tasks
directions.diagnosis: Nearly run (WiSE-FT on CLIP; Mirzadeh 2020; quantization rounding restores old knowledge, Zhang 2024) and confounded: shrinking a delta trades learning for retention by construction (Subramanian 2026, abstract). The informative version is a learning-strength-matched method comparison with no stake in an assumption about minds.

directions.title: Selective ('triage') replay of uncertain or tagged items
directions.diagnosis: Already run: surprise-prioritised replay on Llama-3.1-8B (SuRe, 68.53 vs 50.53 random). Human prior small after bias correction (targeted reactivation g = 0.13). Our variant has no assumption at stake.

directions.title: Forgotten knowledge resurfaces; relearning savings; spacing
directions.diagnosis: Run many times on 7-8B models (Deeb & Roger; Hu; Lynch; Zheng; Jain; Kotha; Jiang; Yang 2024 anticipatory recovery). Kept only as a secondary recovery arm of bmq-d1.

directions.title: Sleep-replay consolidation (Tadros 2022) on a transformer
directions.diagnosis: Not ours: the spiking-conversion and Hebbian method has no transformer version, so this is method work, not a test of a mind; evidence MLP/CNN only; no independent replication found.

directions.title: Mortal computation (Hinton 2022; Ororbia & Friston 2023)
directions.diagnosis: No test exists on an open-weight software model: mortal computation is defined by hardware-bound, non-copyable computation.

directions.title: Importance-weighted consolidation (EWC, synaptic intelligence, memory-aware synapses) on LoRA
directions.diagnosis: Method benchmarking in a crowded field, vision evidence only; simple baselines win under honest evaluation (Farquhar & Gal 2018; van de Ven & Tolias 2019); it asks nothing about a mind.

directions.title: Active forgetting by periodic embedding resets (Chen 2023)
directions.diagnosis: Needs pretraining scale, and is about plasticity for new languages, not retention.

directions.title: Gist and false memory (DRM lures) after consolidation into weights
directions.diagnosis: Nearly run: Spens & Burgess 2026 show semanticisation after LoRA consolidation on Mistral-7B; the human sleep and false-memory effect is null overall (g = 0.13, sign flips with list length).

directions.title: A reconsolidation window for LoRA edits (retrieve, then update)
directions.diagnosis: The human flagship (Schiller 2010) fails principled reanalysis (Chalkia 2020); the knowledge-editing literature was not read; the prediction is worth little.

directions.title: Consolidation protects against interference (A-B in weights, A-C in context)
directions.diagnosis: Does not transfer cleanly: with A-B in weights and A-C in context, the 'correct' answer is set by the question, which is the knowledge-conflict literature (not read), not interference.

directions.title: Facts consistent with the model's priors are learned faster and interfere less (Kumaran 2016)
directions.diagnosis: Probably run in the LLM knowledge-injection literature (not read here; named for a later scout).

directions.title: Fan effect in LLM memory
directions.diagnosis: Not about forgetting, and Llama-3 showed no reliable effect (Roberts 2024).

directions.title: Gold map 7: two-friend local friendliness with external settings on ibm_fez
Gold map 8: a physical baseline for the order-effect instrument, sequential Peres–Mermin
Gold map 11: hardware as an oracle for sampling the model cannot compute

directions.short: Entangled claims: quantum walk vs PageRank
directions.title: Sean's entangled-claims idea: does a quantum walk over program 1's claim graph predict which of its directions were killed and which hit, better than PageRank does?
directions.odds_template: none: stated in one pass by the close-founding session (branch close-founding), not by the scout's v1 fresh-context template; re-elicit with v1 before pre-registration
directions.odds_event: On program 1's claim graph (the directions in map/entangled-mind.json as nodes, parent links and shared-data/replication links as edges), a continuous-time quantum walk started from the known hits and kills, scored leave-one-node-out, predicts each resolved node's outcome (hit 1, killed 0; mixed and open left out) with AUROC higher than personalised PageRank on the same graph and the same seeds, by a bootstrap 95% interval whose lower end is above 0. Quantum counts only if it beats this classical baseline; beating chance alone does not count.
directions.odds_rationale: Program 1 put six quantum-against-classical comparisons on the record (h2, h34, v2, v21, son, e5) and the classical twin matched or won every one: (0+1)/(6+2) = 0.125 by the running-base-rate rule (P1). Lower again because about 25 labelled nodes on a near-tree give little power, and on a tree a quantum walk's ranking and a diffusion's are close. Odds are for beating PageRank, not for beating chance.
directions.question: Can the way program 1's ideas connect to each other, treated as a quantum system, tell which of them were going to fail, better than ordinary link-ranking can?
known: Program 1's quantum-against-classical tests: the classical twin matched or won all six.
The claim graph and every outcome are already in the ledger, so the test costs nothing; the quantum walk is simulated on the laptop, no chip.
directions.cheapest_test: Archive only: build the graph from map/entangled-mind.json and ledger/bets.jsonl, run a simulated continuous-time quantum walk and personalised PageRank from the same seeds, hide one resolved node at a time, and compare the two AUROCs at predicting kill or hit. Pre-register the walk time, the PageRank damping and the edge list before the outcomes are joined.
directions.cost: $0 API; laptop minutes; no chip time (the walk is a simulation, invariant 9)
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth a few minutes of laptop time (free) to treat program 1's ideas as a connected quantum system, and see whether that tells which ideas were going to fail better than ordinary link-ranking (the way search engines rank pages) does? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the quantum version beats ordinary link-ranking, not just chance)?
engine_only: PageRank alone predicts kills and hits above chance (AUROC interval above 0.5): engine odds 0.15
the quantum walk alone predicts above chance: engine odds 0.12 (correlated with the PageRank sub-bet)
